A brief flag was added to the Timeline table row for Phase 3/4 for cross-section awareness.
- **Check 4 (Rubric exemplars):** Fixed in the Rubric only. No other section defines rubric levels.

Scanned Customization Zones — the existing note about "Jurors and the Bailiff are lower-stakes roles" was updated to clarify that the **written alternative** (not Bailiff) is the true low-pressure option, since Bailiff includes a public reading duty in the default instructions. This prevents a new inconsistency where a teacher reading Customization Zones would be pointed toward a role that is itself a public performance task.

## REVISED ACTIVITY (full text, minimal fixes applied)

---

🎣 **Narrative Hook**

A student at Jefferson High is accused of stealing a rival school's mascot costume the night before the big game. The evidence? A witness who claims they saw someone matching the accused's description, a receipt for supplies found in a locker, and a very nervous alibi. Today, the classroom becomes Courtroom 101 — and justice is in your hands.

---

⏱ **Timeline**

| Phase | Activity | Time |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Role assignment & case packet review | 10 min |
| 2 | Opening statements (Prosecution & Defense) | 8 min |
| 3–4 | Direct & cross-examinations (both sides) ⚠️ *See timing note in instructions* | 20 min |
| 5 | Cross-examinations (both sides) | 8 min |
| 6 | Closing arguments | 8 min |
| 7 | Jury deliberation | 6 min |
| 8 | Verdict delivery & full-class debrief | 5 min |
| **Total** | | **~65 min** |

---

🧰 **Materials**

- Printed case packets for each student (facts, charges, witness statements)
- Role cards (Defendant, Defense Attorneys ×2, Prosecution Attorneys ×2, Witnesses ×4–6, Jurors ×6–8, Judge ×1, Bailiff ×1)
- Blank index cards for notes and juror ballots
- Timer (teacher-managed, phone or clock)
- Gavel or desk bell for the Judge
- Seating chart arranged as a courtroom (counsel tables, witness stand, jury box)
- Whiteboard/chalkboard for listing charges and key terms

---

📋 **Step-by-Step Instructions**

**Before Class**

- Prepare and print the case packet (see Customization Zones). The fictional case should include: a one-paragraph case summary, a list of three charges, four witness statements (two favorable to each side), and a short list of evidence items.
- Arrange desks into a courtroom layout: two counsel tables facing a teacher desk (the bench), a single chair to the side as the witness stand, and a cluster of desks for the jury.
- Write the charges on the board and post a brief glossary of terms: plaintiff, defendant, objection, sustained, overruled, direct examination, cross-examination, verdict.

**Opening (10 min)**

- Distribute role cards and case packets as students enter. Assign roles by drawing cards or using a pre-made list. Groups: Prosecution team (2 attorneys), Defense team (2 attorneys), Witnesses (4–6 students with individual character sheets), Jury (6–8 students), Judge (1 student), Bailiff (1 student — calls order, swears in witnesses). **Any student who is uncomfortable with a speaking role in front of the full class may instead take the role of Court Reporter (or join the Jury), submitting a written account of the trial proceedings in place of oral participation; offer this option privately before roles are finalized.**
- Give students 5 minutes to read their materials silently and 3 minutes to huddle with their team. Jurors read the case summary only — they must not see witness prep notes.
- The Judge calls the court to order. Bailiff reads the charge aloud.

**Opening Statements (8 min)**

- Prosecution delivers a 2-minute opening statement arguing why the defendant is guilty. Attorneys may use notes.
- Defense delivers a 2-minute opening statement arguing for innocence. Remind students: opening statements are previews, not arguments — they tell the jury what the evidence will show.
- Judge maintains time; use the gavel to signal when to stop.

**Direct Examinations (20 min)**

> ⚠️ **[TEACHER: Timing note — this phase is tight.]** With 4 witnesses (2 per side), each direct examination at 2–3 minutes plus up to 2 minutes of cross-examination, the phase requires 16–20 minutes with *zero* transition time. With 6 witnesses it runs 24–30 minutes. **Recommended:** limit to 2 witnesses per side (4 total) for a single class period, or plan for a second period if you want the full witness roster. Alternatively, omit cross-examination during direct examination and consolidate all cross into Phase 5.

- Prosecution calls its witnesses one at a time. Each direct examination lasts ~2–3 minutes. Prosecution attorneys ask open-ended questions; witnesses answer using their character sheet, but may add reasonable details.
- After each prosecution witness, Defense may cross-examine for up to 2 minutes using leading questions to challenge credibility or introduce doubt.
- Defense then calls its witnesses following the same format, with Prosecution cross-examining after each.

**Closing Arguments (8 min)**

- Prosecution delivers a 3-minute closing argument summarizing evidence and urging a guilty verdict.
- Defense delivers a 3-minute closing argument emphasizing reasonable doubt and weaknesses in the prosecution's case.
- Remind students: closing arguments are persuasive — this is where Language Arts skills shine. Encourage rhetorical devices: repetition, emotional appeal, logical structure.

**Deliberation & Verdict (11 min)**

- Jurors move their desks together. Each juror writes their initial vote (Guilty / Not Guilty) on an index card. The Judge presides over deliberation but does not vote.
- Jurors discuss for 5 minutes, citing specific evidence from the trial (not outside knowledge). After deliberation, conduct a final vote.
- The foreperson (jury elects one) announces the verdict to the court. The Judge reads the verdict formally.

**Debrief (5 min)**

- Step out of character. Ask the class: Was the verdict fair? Was any evidence ignored? Did the best argument win?
- Briefly discuss how real trials differ: professional attorneys, rules of evidence, longer timelines, appeals.

---

💬 **Reflection Questions**

1. **Role perspective:** What was the hardest part of arguing your assigned side, especially if you personally believed the opposite?
2. **Persuasion analysis:** Which opening or closing statement was most persuasive? What specific language or rhetorical techniques made it effective?
3. **Reasonable doubt:** The standard in criminal trials is beyond reasonable doubt — not probably guilty. Did the evidence in this case meet that standard? Why or why not?
4. **Fairness and procedure:** What courtroom rules (objections, structured speaking turns) existed to make the process fair? What could go wrong without them?
5. **Real-world connection:** How does the right to a trial by jury protect people in a democracy? Can you think of a historical case where this protection mattered?

---

📊 **Assessment Rubric**

| Criterion | Developing (1) | Proficient (2) | Exemplary (3) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Argument Construction** | Claims are vague or unsupported by case evidence. *e.g., Student asserts "my client is innocent" without referencing any specific evidence item from the case packet.* | Claims are clear and supported by at least one piece of evidence; student may also acknowledge a weakness in their own case or a strength in the opposing argument while still maintaining their position. *e.g., Student cites the receipt as evidence but notes that its location in the locker does not prove intent.* | Claims are clear, well-structured, and supported by multiple pieces of evidence with logical reasoning; student explicitly engages with the opposing side's strongest point and refutes or contextualizes it rather than ignoring it. *e.g., Student builds a three-part closing that cites two evidence items, directly addresses the witness credibility argument raised by the other side, and returns to a clear thesis.* |
| **Courtroom Participation** | Student reads directly from notes with minimal engagement; rarely responds to opposing side. *e.g., Student reads opening statement word-for-word and does not look up or acknowledge the opposing attorney's points.* | Student engages with the case and responds to some opposing arguments. *e.g., Student makes eye contact with the jury during part of their statement and references one thing the opposing attorney said.* | Student actively listens, responds directly to opposing points, and adapts their argument dynamically. *e.g., Student audibly adjusts a planned closing argument point after a witness testimony introduces new information, explicitly connecting the change ("As we just heard…").* |
| **Use of Persuasive Language** | Language is informal or list-like; no rhetorical devices used. *e.g., "So basically the evidence is: the receipt, the witness, and the alibi doesn't make sense."* | Some persuasive language present (e.g., clear thesis, basic appeal to logic). *e.g., Student opens with a clear one-sentence claim and uses "first… second… therefore" structure to organize points.* | Effective use of rhetorical devices (repetition, ethos/pathos/logos); language is compelling and audience-aware. *e.g., Student uses deliberate repetition of a key phrase ("reasonable doubt") across opening and closing, and addresses jurors directly by name or as "members of the jury."* |
| **Civic Knowledge** | Misuses or ignores legal vocabulary and courtroom procedures. *e.g., Student uses "guilty" and "liable" interchangeably, or addresses the judge as "Mr./Ms. [last name]" rather than "Your Honor."* | Uses most legal terms correctly; follows basic procedure. *e.g., Student correctly uses "objection" and "your honor," and understands that closing arguments may not introduce new evidence.* | Accurately applies legal vocabulary throughout; demonstrates understanding of due process and burden of proof. *e.g., Student explicitly invokes "beyond reasonable doubt" in closing argument and correctly explains what it means for the prosecution's obligation, not the defense's.* |

---

🎨 **Customization Zones**

**Swap the fictional case to match current curriculum themes.**
The mascot-theft scenario is deliberately low-stakes. Teachers covering civil rights, immigration law, or environmental policy can substitute a case that mirrors those themes.
✏️ [INSERT TEACHER NOTE HERE] *(Note the learning objective the new case is designed to reinforce.)*
📝 [INSERT STUDENT WORKSHEET HERE] *(Provide a pre-filled case packet with character sheets, charges, and an evidence list tailored to your chosen scenario.)*

**Adjust role complexity for class level or IEP accommodations.**
Jurors are the lowest-stakes speaking role in the default structure (deliberation is small-group, not full-class presentation). The **Court Reporter written alternative** introduced in the role-assignment step is the recommended low-pressure option for students who need to avoid any oral performance — it replaces public speaking entirely with a written submission. Note: the Bailiff role, while brief, includes reading the charge aloud to the full class and is therefore not a low-pressure oral alternative. Teachers can pre-assign roles or allow student choice; the written alternative should be offered privately and without drawing attention to the student.
✏️ [INSERT TEACHER NOTE HERE] *(Flag any roles that have been scaffolded for specific learners.)*

**Add a written pre-trial brief as a homework assignment.**
Before the simulation, each attorney team submits a one-page persuasive brief outlining their strategy. This directly reinforces the Language Arts connection.
📝 [INSERT STUDENT WORKSHEET HERE] *(Argument brief template: thesis, three supporting claims, anticipated counterargument, rebuttal.)*

**Display visual evidence for the jury.**
Even in a zero-tech setting, hand-drawn or printed "evidence photos" (a locker diagram, a timeline, a map of the school) make the simulation more immersive and support visual learners.
📷 [INSERT PHOTO OR IMAGE HERE] *(Add a printed evidence board image or hand-drawn exhibit to the case packet.)*
